title: Session Salvage · Illustrated guide
tagline: When a session dies, move the progress out of the chat and into the repository
s1.h: When a session dies, what dies with it
s1.p1: The code does not die. The code is on disk, and in git. What dies is everything that only existed inside that conversation:
s1.li1: The goal — what you were actually trying to build
s1.li2: The ruled-out approaches — tried it, does not work, do not try again
s1.li3: The hard limits — which file must never be touched
s1.li4: The next step — what the last session was about to do
s1.p2: A fresh session gets none of it, so it redoes finished work, or edits the very file you said never to touch. This tool freezes those four things into files in the repository and lets the new session read them itself.
s2.p1: Three triggers — run it if any one appears:
s2.li1: The conversation slows down, tool calls start failing, upstream returns 400 or a provider cutoff notice
s2.li2: You are already wondering whether to start a new session
s2.li3: The vitals check puts a session in the "hand off now" band
s2.p2: The bands are not guesses. They come from the measured distribution of 54 Claude transcripts and 54 Codex transcripts on one machine:
s2.r1: 100% of this band hit a fatal error
s2.p3: "Fatal error" means a signature that actually killed a session: content-blocked, provider cutoff, no available channel, image dimension exceeded. Errors that were merely annoying do not count.
s3.p1: Three entry points, equivalent features. Pick whichever fits your hands:
s3.gui.p: The best looking one. Switch between simplified Chinese, traditional Chinese, and English at any time; light and dark follow the system. The server binds the loopback address only and every request needs a one-shot token — it can run git commit against an arbitrary path, so that is not optional.
s3.menu.p: No flags to remember. Double-click 双击运行.cmd on Windows, run ./scripts/run.sh on Linux and macOS. Drag the project folder into the window to fill the path.
s3.cli.p: Best for scripts. Add --json to make the output machine-consumable.
s4.step1.p: Commits everything in the worktree, except files the plan document declares user-owned. How it recognizes them: the plan says something like "`docs/LOGO.jpg` is a user-owned file and must not be committed", and that path is added to the exclusion list automatically.
s4.step1.note: The exclusion uses git's long :(exclude,literal) form rather than the :!path shorthand. The shorthand is unsupported on older git, and when the path contains [ or * it is treated as a glob, so the exclusion silently fails — and the private file gets committed.
s4.step2.p: Ticks checkboxes from objective evidence, never from anyone's self-report. Only when every file of a task exists and every symbol is genuinely defined by a def / class / function does it tick that task's steps.
s4.step3.p: Produces a handoff Markdown (state, completion, gaps, test results, environment traps) and an opening prompt you can paste straight in.
s4.step4.note: The prompt carries only topic, session id and transcript path; full digests stay in the handoff file - two multi-MB transcripts run to a million characters, which no prompt can hold. Use --pick-sessions to tick interactively, or --sessions PATH to name them directly.
s4.step4.p: After the scan lists your sessions, tick the ones related to this repo. The digest each session wrote itself goes into the handoff document, and the opening prompt names their topic, session id and transcript path, telling the next session to treat those conclusions as established facts rather than re-deriving them. Digests come from Codex compaction records and Claude Code topic titles - primary records, not this tool inferring anything.
s5.h: How it decides something is done
s5.p1: Two kinds of evidence, both independently checkable:
s5.e1.p: The plan's **Files:** block lists which files each task should produce; it checks the disk directly.
s5.e2.p: The **Interfaces:** block lists which symbols should exist, and one composed regex sweeps the whole repository in a single pass — not "the word appears in a file" but "the word actually follows def / class / function / const".
s5.p2: File present but symbol undefined means partial — no tick. That single rule catches the most common false completion: the file was created but it is empty, or it holds one pass.
s5.diagram.title: Verdict flow
s6.h: It stops concurrent writes by itself
s6.p1: Two sessions writing one worktree is the single failure mode that genuinely loses work: our git add buries what they staged, or their commit --amend rewrites the commit we just made.
s6.block.h: Blocking signals — stop by default, exit code 3
s6.block.p: Only another process can cause these:
s6.block.li1: Files already staged that this run did not stage
s6.block.li2: index.lock present — git is writing the index
s6.warn.h: Advisory signals — continue, but record them in the handoff
s6.warn.p: A git-tracked file modified within the last two minutes. The most common cause is you, having just finished editing and come straight here.
s6.why.p: Treating "just edited" as blocking would force --force on every run, and --force waves through the real blocking signals too. That is worse. With the split, --force stays a genuine exception.
s6.after.p: If someone else's commit moved HEAD while it ran, a second session is racing you and the HEAD in the prompt is already stale. The tool warns explicitly and suggests rerunning. Our own two commits are expected and never trigger it — the commit subjects are recognized in all three languages, so switching language does not cause a false alarm.
s6.diagram.title: Concurrency protection flow
s7.h: What is in the prompt, and why
s7.p1: Five blocks. Missing any one of them sends the next session down the wrong path:
s7.b1.p: Repository path, branch, HEAD. Without it the agent does not know where it is.
s7.b2.h: Read the plan first, with the intent sections named
s7.b2.p: Not just "go look at the plan" but naming the Goal / Constraints / Architecture sections. Without it the plan reads as a to-do list and the hard limits get missed.
s7.b3.p: "Do not redo Task 1 / Task 3". A bare number ("12 steps done") is useless — the agent does not know which 12.
s7.b4.p: Which file is missing, which symbol is missing. Without it the agent starts the search from scratch.
s7.b5.p: Generation time plus the matching HEAD. Without it an old prompt gets reused, pointing at a state that no longer exists.
s7.diagram.title: The prompt's five blocks
s8.h: Prompts expire — do not reuse an old one
s8.p1: The prompt ends with its generation time and HEAD. Once the repository takes new commits, the state it describes is wrong: the "priority" and "gaps" it names may already be resolved, and the HEAD it cites may have been rebased away.
s8.p2: Rerunning takes seconds. The cost of reusing an old prompt is a new session acting on an out-of-date map.
s9.h: What a plan document looks like
s9.p1: Auto-detected: the newest markdown within depth 5 that has task headings and at least three checkboxes. You can also name one with --plan.
s9.p2: Both of Task 1's files must exist and both symbols must genuinely be defined before the two steps get ticked.
s10.exit.2: Bad argument or environment (path missing, not a git repository, git not found)
s10.exit.3: Stopped because a concurrent write was detected; nothing was changed
s11.c1.p: Project name, paths, task names, and test commands are all inferred from the repository. Point it at another project and not one line changes.
s11.c2.p: When a step fails — no ripgrep, a test timeout, an unreadable submodule — it degrades and writes out what it did get, rather than leaving the whole handoff empty-handed.
s11.c3.p: The prompt is pasted into the new session, so it consumes context by existing. Long material goes into the handoff file for the agent to read itself.
s12.p: With no plan document in the project, the original intent cannot be transmitted. File existence and symbol definitions can say how far the work got, but not what it was for. The tool tells you plainly to add a goal by hand. That is not a bug; the information simply is not there.
